```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  warning = FALSE,
  comment = "#>",
  root.dir = './'

```
The previous tutorials stop at the field: they show how to estimate the ligand-receptor
interaction as a spatial vector field, and how to score and visualise it. This one asks a
transcriptional question:

**Along the direction in which a ligand-receptor pair signals, which genes change their
expression?**

Answering it means treating a field quantity as a trajectory. Take one LR pair and look at
its field potential `U`: every spot now sits at some position on the ligand-to-receptor axis,
and gene expression can be modelled as a function of that position. We use
[tradeSeq](https://github.com/statOmics/tradeSeq) to fit that function, which is why it is
listed as a suggested dependency of spWAVE.

## Setup

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(magrittr)
library(dplyr)

library(Seurat)
library(ggplot2)
library(spWAVE)
```

## Rebuild the field

We reuse the 10x Visium mouse brain dataset and the small TGFb/FGF database from the
[first tutorial](Field_est2.html), so the field values here are the same ones. The field
takes a few seconds; the trajectory fit below takes several minutes.

```{r field, cache = TRUE, message = FALSE}
#** folder holding the tutorial dataset, adjust it to your local copy
data_dir <- "../../data"
brain <- readRDS(file.path(data_dir, "mouse_brain_anno_clu.rds"))

mouse_db <-
  load_database(db_source = "CellChat", db_species = "mouse", filter_type = "Secreted")
#** a smaller subset, as in the field tutorials
mouse_db %<>% dplyr::filter(Family %in% c("TGFb", "FGF"))

brain_spWAVE <- create_spWAVE_object(brain, mouse_db, assay = "SCT")
brain_spWAVE <- brain_spWAVE %>% perform_LR_field_calc()
```

## The trajectory is the field itself

Extracting one LR pair gives a data.frame with the field vector (`Ex`, `Ey`), the field
potential (`U`), the ligand and receptor expression, and their difference.

```{r extract}
fgf1 <- perform_field_extract(brain_spWAVE, "Fgf1.Fgfr1")
fgf1 %>% head
```

`U` is what we will use as the trajectory: the question is which genes, in the space
the field potential lays out, are expressed along the way that space is arranged -- so
`U` goes in as the trajectory variable. Two things are worth being explicit about:

- **it is not a lineage pseudotime.** Nothing is inferred about cell state ordering;
  `U` is a spatial quantity, and cells with the same potential are simply "equally far"
  along the ligand-to-receptor direction. Every cell joins the same single trajectory,
  which is why the cell weights are all 1.
- **the sign has a direction.** A ligand field contributes positively to the potential and
  the receptor field negatively, so genes going up along `U` are the ones tracking the
  ligand side of the interaction.

The column name is itself an argument: `traj_arg` accepts any column of this data.frame,
so `Ex`, `Ey` or `E_strength` can be used the same way. Which of them to hand it is a
question about how you read the field space -- the direction of the field, or only how
strong it is -- rather than about the method.

## Fit the trajectory

The fit is the expensive step of this tutorial, so the call is shown here rather than run.
The chunk after it loads a result computed in advance.

```{r tradeseq, eval = FALSE, message = FALSE}
brain_fgf1 <- run_LR_tradeSeq(
  seurat_obj = brain,
  database_result = brain_spWAVE,
  LR = "Fgf1.Fgfr1",
  kept_db = brain_spWAVE@kept_db,
  traj_arg = "U",
  nknots = 6,
  parallel = TRUE,
  paral_workers = 2
)
```

Two things decide the cost: the fit covers every gene of the assay, not only the ligand and
the receptor, and `paral_workers` trades memory for time rather than being a free speedup.

```{r load fit, message = FALSE}
#** the object the call above returns
brain_fgf1 <- readRDS(file.path(data_dir, "fgf1_trade_res.rds"))
```

The returned list carries both the fitted model and the `field_df` it was built from;
the second is not optional, because the plotting step below needs it.

## Test genes along the trajectory

```{r gene test, message = FALSE}
fgf1_test <- run_tradeSeq_gene_test(brain_fgf1$trade_res, method_use = "association")
fgf1_test %>% head
```

`run_tradeSeq_gene_test` wraps the two tradeSeq tests: `"association"` asks whether a
gene's expression changes at all along the trajectory, `"startvsend"` only asks whether
the two ends of the trajectory differ. Both fill the genes whose GAM did not converge
with neutral values instead of dropping them, and both report BH-adjusted p-values.

The test here is deliberately permissive -- thousands of genes come back significant --
because it tests a spatial gradient over a few thousand spots, not a designed contrast.
Rank genes by `waldStat`, rather than reading the p-value column as a list of
discoveries. The table comes back sorted by it, so the top of it is the ranking; we carry
the first 200 genes into the figures below.

```{r top genes}
top_genes <- head(rownames(fgf1_test), 200)
```

## Visualise the trajectory genes

```{r heatmap, fig.retina = 2, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 9, fig.align = "center", message = FALSE}
ht_main <- plot_tradeTest_heatmap(
  brain_fgf1$trade_res,
  fgf1_test,
  brain_fgf1$field_df,
  select_genes = top_genes,
  n_split_row = 4,
  title = "Fgf1 -> Fgfr1 along the field potential"
)
```

Rows are genes, columns are positions along the trajectory, and the colour is expression
after `predictSmooth` has evaluated each gene's GAM at 100 points and each row has been
scaled. So a row is not "expression in a cell" but "the shape of this gene's response".
The `Potential` annotation bar underneath is the trajectory itself: mid grey is `U = 0`,
blue is negative, red is positive. That is what makes the figure readable -- a gene block
that brightens towards the red end is induced on the ligand side.

The rows are split into `n_split_row` blocks (4 by default) by k-means on the response
shapes, and that is where the biology shows up: with these 200 genes the two largest
blocks -- 75 and 62 genes -- run in opposite directions, one rising towards the ligand
side, one falling towards the receptor side. The rows carry no labels because 200 gene
names do not fit; the two blocks are read back out of this figure below and drawn on
their own, with their names shown.

`select_genes` takes any gene list, so the same call shows an arbitrary set of genes by
name -- it masks both `top_n_gene` and `order_by`. The two block figures below are drawn
that way.

## What the trajectory genes are

Each block is a group of genes with the same response shape, so the blocks are the natural
unit to test. They do not have to be recovered by clustering again: the split is already
in the figure, and `row_order()` reads the members of each block straight off it.

```{r blocks}
#** row_order() indexes the rows of the matrix the heatmap was drawn from, which is the
#** gene vector that was passed in -- so the block members are read off by position
block_genes <- ComplexHeatmap::row_order(ht_main) %>% lapply(function(i) top_genes[i])
lengths(block_genes)

#** the two largest blocks, labelled by the direction their mean response runs in
yhat   <- tradeSeq::predictSmooth(brain_fgf1$trade_res, gene = top_genes, nPoints = 100, tidy = FALSE)
scaled <- t(scale(t(yhat)))
big <- names(sort(lengths(block_genes), decreasing = TRUE))[1:2]
rise <- sapply(big, function(b) { p <- colMeans(scaled[block_genes[[b]], , drop = FALSE]); p[100] - p[1] })
big <- big[order(-rise)]
names(big) <- ifelse(sort(rise, decreasing = TRUE) > 0, "rising (ligand side)", "falling (receptor side)")
names(big)
```

The two blocks run in opposite directions, so each is worth looking at on its own. One
figure per block, with the members of that block as `select_genes` and their names shown;
the two are drawn side by side.

```{r block heatmaps, fig.retina = 2, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 9, fig.show = "hold", out.width = "50%", message = FALSE}
block_ht <- Map(function(genes, label)
  plot_tradeTest_heatmap(
    brain_fgf1$trade_res,
    fgf1_test,
    brain_fgf1$field_df,
    select_genes  = genes,
    show_rownames = TRUE,
    n_split_row   = 1,
    title         = paste0("Block: ", label)
  ),
  block_genes[big], names(big))
```

Then a plain over-representation test per block. The universe is the set of genes that were
actually fitted, not the genome: a whole-genome background would report the expression
filter as if it were enrichment.

```{r enrich, message = FALSE}
library(clusterProfiler)
library(org.Mm.eg.db)   # Bioconductor mouse annotation

block_enrich <- lapply(big, function(b)
  enrichGO(block_genes[[b]], OrgDb = org.Mm.eg.db, keyType = "SYMBOL", ont = "BP",
           universe = rownames(fgf1_test), pAdjustMethod = "BH",
           pvalueCutoff = 0.05, qvalueCutoff = 0.2, readable = TRUE))
```

```{r enrich plot, fig.retina = 2, fig.width = 18, fig.height = 9, fig.align = "center"}
library(enrichplot)
library(patchwork)
wrap_plots(Map(function(eg, l) dotplot(eg, showCategory = 15) + ggtitle(l),
               block_enrich, names(big)), ncol = 2)
```

Each block comes back as one family and no term appears in both: the rising block is myelin
and oligodendrocyte terms (ensheathment of neurons, myelination, oligodendrocyte
differentiation), the falling block is synaptic terms (synapse organization, postsynaptic
membrane potential, glutamate receptor signalling). `U` is a spatial axis, so a block that
tracks it also tracks anatomy -- here the positive end is hindbrain, the negative end
hippocampus and cortex.
